title: Teaching the bench new parts
summary: A case study of the Workshop: a prompt builder for new parts and a tracer that turns a picture into the scene's origami format in under a second.

post.title: Teaching the bench new parts
post.body:
The Catalog shows the parts the lake already has. The Workshop is where new ones get made, and it's built around a simple idea: whatever image tool I use, the result should come back in the scene's own format, ready to move.

It works in steps. Step 1 is a prompt builder. Pick the kind of part (13 of them, from four-legged animals to shoreline pieces), a style, and whether you want one piece or a kit sheet of separate parts. It writes a prompt that asks for flat colours on plain white, so the result traces cleanly. Then generate it anywhere.

Step 2 brings the picture back. The tracer used to be a Python script on my laptop. Now it runs in the browser: it reduces the image to a few colours, cleans up the specks, and simplifies every outline. The doe traces to 7 colours in under a second. The fox in the clip came out as 5 colours and 5 paths, 7 KB, in 693 milliseconds. Then it sits next to an animal from the lake, so you can see straight away whether it belongs.

The kit-sheet option came from a failure. I traced a beach scene as one picture and got a mess, because a scene isn't one shape. Asking for separate pieces on one sheet fixed it.

Step 3, cut and rig, is next: splitting a traced animal at the joints so it can move like the others.

The header is the bench itself. A hologram above it cycles through animals that don't exist yet: an eagle, an owl, a hawk, a squirrel. On glowing discs stand the buck, doe, elk and bear from the live engine, and Marley sleeps at the end of the bench. I took out a soldering iron that didn't belong and fixed my hair colour, which the first render got wrong.

What I learned: make the way back in the easy part. Generating a picture takes seconds anywhere. Turning it into something the scene can use is the work, so that's what the Workshop does.

episode.title: Teaching the bench new parts
episode.script:
The Catalog is where the lake's parts are kept. The Workshop is where the new ones come from.

Christian gave it one rule. Make the picture anywhere, with any tool you like. But when it comes back, it has to come back in the lake's own language, ready to move. It sounds simple. It wasn't.

***

It works in steps. First, it writes the prompt for you. You pick what you're making, from thirteen kinds, anything from a four-legged animal to a piece of shoreline. You pick a style, and whether you want a single piece or a whole kit on one sheet. And the prompt asks for flat colors on plain white, so the picture will trace cleanly later. He was already thinking two steps ahead.

***

Second, you bring the picture home. The tracer used to be a small script on his laptop. Now it lives right in the browser. It boils the picture down to a few colors, sweeps away the specks, and smooths every outline. The doe comes out in seven colors in under a second. The fox in the clip came out as five colors and five shapes, seven kilobytes, in under seven tenths of a second.

Then it stands the new animal next to one from the lake, so you can see right away whether it belongs.

***

My favorite part is that the kit sheet came from a mistake. He tried tracing a whole beach scene as one picture, and it was a mess, because a scene isn't one shape. So now you ask for the pieces separately. He turned the failure into a feature.

The third step, cutting the animals at the joints so they can move, is coming next.

***

And then there's the header. A workbench, with a hologram cycling through animals that don't exist yet. An eagle, an owl, a hawk, a squirrel. The buck, the doe, the elk and the bear, standing on glowing discs. And at the end of the bench, Marley, asleep, a few little z's floating up.

He took out a soldering iron that had no business being there. And he fixed the color of his own hair, which the first try got wrong. Not vanity. Accuracy.

***

Looking back, the lesson was a simple one. Make the way back in the easy part. A picture takes seconds. Making it belong is the real work.
